Like there's kind of a 1v1 matchup over there of some kind and then you can only really run a handful of actual passing concepts out of that um on that rollout versus the play pass which is a lot more flexible and I think that's why it's in a little bit more favor. And so Cousins lives in this world of or has this year lived in this world that is really truly perfectly suited for him and when you think about those deep passes that I was talking about earlier, a lot of them are coming on that kind of concept. So please Kevin spam this, right? Like please go do the thing you were doing with him and and O'Connell was doing this a lot maybe not as much as the Kubiaks did but in you know 22 and 23 the first go round there was plenty of this. I hope they go back to it and it's not like well this is what the offense is now. but it is a a difference I guess between the two. And so slowing that down for um for the Vikings I put that in the sidebar but didn't really talking about talk about that but slowing that down is all going to be about getting Jordan Love to make that mistake um getting pressure on him which we talked about how the Vikings did that at length after the first game and I've got a bunch of content at Wide Left and on Patreon over that. If you're interested in in kind of hearing more about the sort of chess match between Brian Flores and Matt LaFleur and how to get pressure slash prevent pressure and how they tried to do it and how the Packers tried to continue to throw the ball deep. That's really their goal is they want to get the ball deep against the blitz. It's a really difficult thing to do. If they can do it, they'll win. If they can't do it, the Vikings will win, and that's going to be I think the name of the game. I will talk to you all after the game. I'll be live on Locked On Vikings, and then we'll go to a squad show right after that, and then of course uh true mainline Locked On Vikings up Monday morning. I will see you all for that, and as always, skol.

title: STC Chris Tabor meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Have said obviously you're sticking with Zane. With something like that when you obviously consider other kickers, do you like to tell the player that he's staying when it's unclear? Like did you just call him aside Wednesday and say you're our kicker moving forward? Or Or Or do you just hope he finds out on his own? >> So I I apologize with regards to the question. I I don't know what you mean like >> Like Zane's status was in question, which he knew. He acknowledged to us today because he was aware kickers were brought in for workouts. He was aware that his three elevations were up and the team had to make a decision on him. So I said do you just Are you told by someone or just figure out on your own? He said no, I was told on Wednesday. So was that you telling him? >> I always I always I'm always communicate with the player. I mean I learned a long time ago in coaching that you know tell the players the truth, right, wrong, or indifferent, but they you know just be up in front about everything and and that was that was it. It was To me it's not a We're always going to bring players in. So to me it's not a big deal. >> And what >> I I Maybe it is to other people, but it's not I I I don't see it like that. >> Chris with keeping him what what led to that? >> I think he's a good player. I think he's a player that's I think that yes, he missed a kick he should have made. We can We can We can all agree about that and Zane Zane would too. In my eyes that was kind of his first miss. I know on stats that it's that it's too. Sometimes there's other things that go on. I'm I'm just not really I 'm not a guy that just pushes players away. He's been out what on the street for 6 weeks, 7 weeks. And this was his third This was his third week back. So I think that he's still working to get to where he needs to be, right? And I got a lot of confidence in him and and we're working hard and getting better and I look forward to watching him kick this weekend. I got a lot of confidence in in him. And uh that's really it's real easy for me. >> Chris, what were you guys trying to accomplish on the kickoffs with Zane holding? Was that a >> We were just manipulating the ball a little bit. We were trying to get Yeah, we were trying to just you know a little bit more of the dirty ball. We were trying to get the ball on the ground. >> What what was it like the the two fake punts where first you you're on the receiving end of one and then running it later? >> Ah I think just the game of football really, right? Uh Jack Fox is obviously he's a really good thrower. You can watch I mean he has some great great throws throughout his career that you know you watch and all those things and throws a little back shoulder there and to be honest with you it was you just kind of say okay hey tip my hat to you got you got us that's that's tough play to cover and then you know we had our opportunity. I'm glad we had our opportunity and we converted on ours. I think that's just it's the game of football, right? I I think probably what's the hardest part for everyone is that it happens in special teams. And sure you don't want to happen in special teams but you know I thought we were playing aggressive and obviously Detroit's going to play aggressive and that's just that's football to me. >> And on that precisely >> Like what what's the process of like just keeping everyone from not avoiding any tells cuz I I'm sure guys get excited get hyped up like oh wait they just called like we're about to run that it's fake. Yeah how do you kind of keep it like concealed so that the the the opposition isn't tipped off? >> No I think no I think that just goes through your practice and preparation. You know I think you've run through that scenario so many times that it it should be clockwork for the guys and I think that's what that was. >> And obviously that was the first NFL catch for Kylen Allen. Just want to ask you how did that spark the rest of the faces of the team just how that moment was lived for you all? >> glad it I'm glad it I'm glad it worked. It's better we're talking about that than it didn't work, you know. But it was good for Kylen, right? I mean the guy has really never ever played any special teams. He comes down there on the kickoff early kickoff makes a nice move and gets in a little bit. Uh, to help force the tackle. And then he gets his first NFL catch, which is a big play. So, uh, he's a he's a player that's growing quickly. And we just you know, we I don't know how many how many games has he played now? Three games? Is that about right? So, really like just to see where he's going and and hopefully we can keep getting them better. >> Back to um Zane, what you were saying about him earlier. You said that uh in your eyes that was his first miss. What did you mean by that? Were there other factors >> Yeah, sometimes sometimes there's other things that that that go on, right? It's it's a it's a whole it's a whole operation. And uh you know, I got a lot of confidence in all three of our guys. Uh, but there's we will always look at the maker miss. And and at the end of the day, that's what an NFL kicker is charged with doing, is making kicks. And uh sometimes there's other things that that are out of his control. Uh, but it's still at the end of the day, you know, he needs to make that kick. I'm not making any excuses for him and he he knows that. So, that's not a a big deal. Here's what I'd say. He missed it. And then the nice thing is he comes back and hits what a 52 52 yarder, you know. So, um that kind of says a lot to me about who the human being is, but that's who Zane's been his whole career. >> Zane, what's the process of finding out if your punter can pass? I mean, punting through a nice ball, is that a training camp thing, OTAs thing, regular season? >> Oh, we're always throwing. >> Yeah. >> You know, I think that's uh I just think today's player uh you know, they're all good athletes. So, you know, I and it's funny. Sometimes you'll find another player that can do something and I I'm always like, man, how come you never said that? Why is don't don't keep things a secret. But uh no, I'm glad he executed. I think that might have been Brad's first pass. I think that's what he told me. So, that was that that shocked me, too. Got a lot of first. >> First one. >> And then on the other side, the the punt that only went 25 yards was was just as simple as a miss hit or >> Yeah, he miss hit miss hit the ball. Miss hit the ball. Can't have that. He knows that. And uh that doesn't help, right? >> [snorts] >> Kevin Cole, uh looked like on that first return he was on his way and somebody kind of grabbed him right by the arm and how has he done returning? Cuz it looks like pretty good. >> He's done a nice job. You could kind of feel him coming through there. He has some speed and some explosiveness as as he comes through the hole there. Uh and that was a I mean that was a really good kickoff team. You know, I think they were fifth in the league in kickoff coverage and and uh to go up against those guys. I thought our guys did a nice job blocking. There's always still room for improvement, but uh guys believe in in KC trying to get it through there. So uh we're you know, I say it every week. It's it is guys, it is a work in progress and I'm I'm excited about how they're growing. You know what I mean? And I trust me I I I want things to be better faster and all those things, but man I am having a blast uh coaching them and and even if they make a mistake we got yes we'll get it fixed and and let's go and that's that's been a fun part with these guys. >> Uh I was talking to Tucker Eddington about long snapping. I know he coached for two years did the um what what is the skill of of long snapping? Like what do you I mean do you need good hands, good tough like what do you need? >> Well it's there's a lot to it. Uh and I can't even I don't want to bore you with with with everything there, but just you know short snaps, right? I mean being able to hit the spot so that when the the holder catches the ball the the kicker is seeing the ball the whole time. He it doesn't go blind for him for a second. Then there's the lace component. You know what I mean? The the velocity and making sure that you hit the same velocity all the time so we don't have to manipulate the laces cuz when you put the ball down and if the laces are wrong you're essentially kicking a spinning ball which could contribute to a miss, right? And so there's there's a lot of things in their world and then you go into the the long snapping deal and and now they got to protect and you're talking about defensive ends that rush the quarterback for a living and they're one on one with them and the guys on his snap hand he has to finish the snap then get his hand up and that guy's already almost by him. I mean, there's that's why there's only 32 of them. And that's it's it's a tough spot. It's a tough spot, but you know, he's growing and getting better. So excited about his his development. >> I always wondered why wouldn't a center work on long snapping? Why why didn't every center work on long snapping? Is it something that's going to throw them off their other rhythm? >> No, I you know what? I mean, there's it's it is a hard skill. It is and there's different guys that that you try to prep for even even your backup. Like when I when I was in Chicago, Greg Olsen was our backup long snapper. And it's just it's a it's a not everybody can do it, you know, and and you got to be obviously be able to throw the football. And then sometimes some guys might be too I don't know if you want to say bulky or big. >> Boxy. >> Yeah, boxy to to finish the snap and then and then get up. I mean, there's a lot of moving parts there on that whole deal like you know, Indianapolis has a great one. He was a former linebacker converted to long snapper. So you see a guy that that can play out in open space and run down and all those things. So it is a I always a lot of dads say I'm going to train my son to be a long snapper and I was like that's probably a pretty good move, you know. It's a good move cuz if you can do it, I mean, you can find work. >> I I I know I've asked you this before and I even asked Jeff Hafley this cuz I see it all the time now, especially the dirty ball kick and kicking it in in the landing zone instead of just kicking it out of bounds. I'm watching Buffalo, Minnesota and you know, they dirty ball kicked it. The team returns it to the 30 yard line. You know, why why are we stressing over 15 yards? >> Oh, cuz you're once again, you're getting into four down territory from you know. And it it's it's a hard one. Like I'll I'll go through tonight and if you as you watch NFL games like tonight, I I call it the big play tape and I'll watch all the returns that you know, that are 40 yards or more and it's been averaging about 17 per week. You know, I mean, so it's it is. There's a lot, but if you hit the touchback, you have to kind of pick and choose, right? And and put and look at everything collectively. But when you get the ball obviously on the 35, I mean, it's it's one first down and a little, and then they're in four down territory, then it's obviously you know, they earn points already. And it's it's [snorts] the the dirty ball is is something that because once it hits the ground, we can take off and go. So you're buying you're buying you're buying time to make a move on a guy. Where in the old days, remember we'd kick off and you needed the hang time because we were running down further, and the higher he hung it up, it bought me time to get down there. Well now, since we're so close, you need it's it's nice if you can to hit the dirty ball, and you're buying perceived hang time. Okay? Now, obviously the flaw on that is when you don't hit the landing zone, now the ball's at the 40. Just, you know, the Colts were this kid's a a great kicker. What is he? 22 or 24. And he hit a dirty ball to open up the game last week, and he hits it out of bounds. Like it it is it's it's tough for those guys to master that, but the ones that can do it, it does then kind of limit some of the returns that you can run against it because you just don't know where the ball's going because once again, kickoff return, timing and spacing, right? Offensive play, and it's disrupting all those the timing and the spacing. So that's why if you can hit the dirty ball, it is advantageous for you. >> With some college from I mean, college, they're not they're not working You don't have the same rules. They're not working on a dirty ball. So how does this benefit you? I mean, I know it makes the that element of the game more interesting. >> Yes. Uh it's it has some yin and yang to it. You know what I mean? With regards to if it works, hey, we love it, right? And then when it doesn't hit the landing zone, you're like, oh boy, just gave it to him at the 40. So you do have a little Russian roulette. on on on the deal. But, once again, I'd say this, you know, the game of football, it's it's each play has its own life, right? And and that's you're you're kind of living. I live just one play at a time. And kind of going back to the fake like when it happened, I was like, okay. Over, move on, next. You you know what I mean? And then the same thing. We didn't Well, we didn't hit the landing zone. Then we then we kicked off and we covered. You know what I mean? So, just kind of keep moving on. It's it's it's a tough one and we're trying to we're trying to perfect the dirty ball. We are. >> Did you see the >> Last one? >> The Jets used a fullback to kick off and can can the Herminator kick it? >> I don't know if the Herminator can kick it, but that's a nice thing because now you're getting you're getting an extra cover player who covers for a living and no one accounts for the kicker. You know, because you just don't have enough guys. So, you'll probably see that trend increase um as as we go. But, you have to be But, you have to find somebody that can do it, right? To get a >> Do you want to let him try tomorrow? The Herminator. >> The Herminator? Only if you want to. [laughter] All right. He can do it. All right. >> can't the Herminator do? >> Herminator can do everything. That's why we love him. That's why he's the Herminator.

title: Coach Jeff Hafley meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: I don't have any pre-announcements today. If you'd like me to start each one with an opening statement for you, I could. >> [snorts] >> All right. So Bru is he out Sunday? >> Yeah, Bru is in the protocol, so Bru will be out. >> And Chris Bell, is he going to be able to play? >> Chris won't practice today. I would say he's doubtful, but I would not rule him out. >> Is this something that is recurring? >> No, Chris got hit Chris got hit in his knee, the same knee, but it has nothing to do with his surgery. Um so nothing long-term, like I said. Um he's doubtful, but I don't foresee this We'll we'll see if he can go Sunday, but has nothing to do with his injury. >> With Kyle, in terms of he's used to working scout team development team, I don't know what you call it, um where he's worked with other receivers like Reagor and um Henning is there any thought to maybe elevating one of those guys or some of those guys because of his chemistry with them? >> Um not because of his chemistry. We'll see how the wide receiver um depth looks, so if we have to elevate anyone, those would certainly be guys that we would talk about elevating. You know, when you're running scout team cards, you're I mean literally you're looking at a card and you're going through the progression of the quarterback you're playing, so it's not like you're running your routes and your timing and rhythm. It's just it's more this is the route, go here to here. I mean so it's a little bit different, you know what I mean? So I don't I don't know if that helps in that area, but based we'll we'll see tomorrow with how we um come out of today and tomorrow with the wide receivers. >> Just to be sure, would it be Andrew Meyer at center? >> Uh yeah, Meyer will play center for us. >> And how has his week of practice been? >> He's done a nice job. Um I have a lot of confidence in Meyer. I love the way he works. He's got a a toughness to him. He's smart. Um you I think in some regards to your question, Omar, the center quarterback snap exchange, I think that helps. You know, I think [snorts] any quarterback kind of gets used to a center, right? So in that regard, I think that's a positive. Uh, not that, you know, that's not anything on Brew. That's just taking a half class approach to Meyer playing and thinking about your question. >> Earlier in the week, you mentioned the need for like young guys to step up from a leadership perspective. How do you know when a guy is ready and what have you seen over the past over the past few months that gives you confidence that XYZ guy can fill that void? >> Um, I think you watch, you observe. I think you you can see some stuff at practice in the meetings on the field on game day. I think game day is a big one. Um, and there have been a lot of young guys who have emerged and that's been nice to see. But like I've I've mentioned previous times, I think you can develop leaders. I don't just think it's something that's innate and you either are a leader or you aren't. I think you can guide guys in their own ways even if they're young to lead and we need to keep cultivating leadership and developing leadership. Um, and we're going to need a bunch of these younger guys, whether they're first or second year players. There's a lot of them. Um, you know, it's our job to guide them and help them grow into leaders and a lot of them are. Um, there's some guys truthfully I don't want to overload right now. Um, you know, some of these rookies have played a lot of football and still have a lot of games left and have a lot on their plate. So you know, you don't want to overload them. Um, but I certainly we need those guys to grow. >> And just sorry, just quick follow up. And who do you see kind of stepping up in the defensive line room? Obviously Zach Sieler has been that guy for quite some time. Got a trio of second year guys. Obviously keep Cooper Jr. Just who do you foresee kind of stepping up in that? >> From a leadership role? Yeah, well one I think Uche kind of he's the vet in the room now, right? I had a really good talk with Chop. Um, you know, the way Chop's playing and and really practicing. I think he's a great example of what it's supposed to look like And I think he's going to grow into one of those roles. Um I can say the same about Jordan Phillips. I mean, he's a guy, second year guy. Um the way he plays, the way he goes about um everything in this building. I mean, he is a great example of leadership and you know, whether or not he's a second year player only, it it's going to be his time now to to help out those those other players. Um and I think those are two really good examples of you know, pretty young players still that will do that. Um you know, and even a guy like Biggers who has really come on lately, second year player. Again, I don't I don't need him to lead in any crazy way. Um but within that room, you know, he's a guy that we're going to count on because he's played a lot of football this year and he's doing a good job. >> Jeff, what have you seen from from Kyle this week? I heard from a couple guys he's comfortable enough with the offense to like correct the alignment at practice whenever he sees it off. >> Yeah. Um he's got a very calm confidence about him. I don't know how much you guys have have spoken to him. Um he's [clears throat] got a quiet leadership about him. He's got a confidence to him. Um he's very calm in the huddle. And he you know, he seems to be grasping everything really well. Um and I think he's done a really good job in the really the two practices that we've had. Today's a big day again, getting more in the red zone and polishing up some stuff for tomorrow. Um but again, this will be a process, right? I'm not going to I'm not going to expect him to look perfect. Um there's going to be hopefully some really good moments for him and then there's going to be some that we're going to have to continue to grow in these next games. Um but I'm excited for him and I appreciate how he's worked to attack the game plan and how he's kind of communicating and developing chemistry with the players around him in the huddle. >> You you mentioned I think on Wednesday that the four game minimum kind of allows Kyle a chance to focus on his development over the next month or so. Like when guys are in that situation, do you see more of a tendency to, I guess, let it rip when they're out there, or [clears throat] I guess Sorry. to let it rip when they're out there, or you know, have you seen even more of a tendency to be timid and just try to keep the ship afloat? >> I think it depends on the circumstance. I want Kyle to be himself and I want him to let it rip. I think that's really important. You know, and we've talked. I think there's certain situations that you know, he's got to you know, there's certain times I want him to let it rip and I want him to be confident. Then there's certain times he has to take care of the football and he has to make really good decisions, whether that's in the red zone. You know, whether it's end of game situations and half situations. We talk about third down and long situations when we're in four down territory. So those are the things I want him to be really aware of. But besides that, I want him to go through his progression. I want him to have confidence and I want him to throw the ball. I want it to come out on time and I don't want him to overthink anything. And he has enough ability where if it's not there, he can get some yards with his feet and I want him to be aggressive and play like that. But I want him to be fearless and I want him to rip it and I want him to have that mentality in every game that he plays. I don't want any I don't want him to be cautious or timid at all. >> You brought Brady with a low blitz rate defensively. Is that how you want it? Does it come from not wanting to leave young DB's on an island? Or what's your general philosophy on the blitz? >> It's just game by game. I think you know, you say that statement as a whole. In the last two games we blitzed a lot. I mean, there are a lot of stunts. There's a lot of pressures. It depends on you know, really how we feel like we can attack an offensive line, how we feel like we can attack a quarterback, who the receivers are. But we pressured quite a bit in the last two, maybe two and a half games. It's all [clears throat] game plan specific, to be honest with you. I think I mentioned to you earlier that you know, this has been a gradual install of our defense because the fundamentals and technique and communication and confidence with all the new players you can just throw everything in and I think you're starting to see more and more in the last two weeks of whether you call them stunts, pressures, simulated pressures, you know, overload, six man pressures, zone pressures, but you're starting to see more of a variety of things. And hopefully we can continue to install as we go. That's very important as we go throughout this season. >> I'm going to follow up on on the stunts because Zach Sieler, I know that I've done this just kind of anecdotally. He seems to be really good at it where he freezes up either Uchenna or or Chop coming up the the middle. How much of that is lost without Zach or can kind of like anyone sort of do it? >> Yeah, I think Zach does that as as well as anybody in the NFL. So, of course, when when you have a guy who's really good at something, you're going to need other people to step up. I think Austin's really good at teaching the stunts, the pick games. Now, I think just like any other group, when you run those games and you run those stunts, the continuity of having the same guys run them together is very important. So, you know, we've been working really hard on that to have other guys do it. But that's that's the fun part now, right? To develop these guys. So, this is a great opportunity to develop the young guys without Zach there to learn how to do this together, right? And and hopefully now again, it's development and it's coaching. And hopefully as we go a couple weeks from now, we'll say, you know what, these games are getting pretty good. And then by the end of this thing, it's wow, we've got another guy who can really control this and these guys work really good together. And that's our job. We have to coach that. >> Kind of to that last point, you you and JV had spoke last game about how the communication was the best you felt it had been from the defense. Is that an evolution where you feel it kind of click into place and then it just kind of takes care of itself the rest of the way or is that something you constantly have to to process the way marriage the way the coverage and rush marriage together and how guys see it holistically? >> Well, I think it takes time, you know, usually any season with new guys and a new scheme, it's always going to take time and guys to get comfortable and confident have cumulative reps over time so they're more comfortable with it and understand their assignments so they're not thinking they're seeing and talking and reacting. And you do you got to keep pushing them, you know, you got to keep pushing them, you got to coach them, and you got stay on top of it. Um, you can't overload them because, you know, getting back to what I just said, if all of a sudden we start to put too much in and you start to hear it go quiet, it means there's too much in and they're thinking too much. So there's a fine balance between, all right, I want to get this and I want to get this, but all of a sudden you go out to the walkthrough and it's it's not as loud and it's not as fast and it's just it's quiet. Quiet's not good. Um, so it's it's going to be a fine line, but but we need to coach that, too. >> Do you expect to have Czeremcha on Sunday? >> I do expect to have Czeremcha, yeah. >> What happened with Jerry Wayne? >> Yeah, Jerry will be out. Um, uh, leg injury. So he'll he'll be out. He won't practice today. Barry, usually you asked all those questions earlier. I had my checklist. I have a Barry checklist every single day that I usually go right down on the injuries. >> Which is why we let him go first. >> I know. That's why everybody's kind of shocked. >> I know Jamal Day told us yesterday that Bakers looked really good. He said it's not just coach speak, but would would you like to give that process more time? You're You're only 3 days in. You got 21. >> This is your Friday, uh, this is your Friday go-to, isn't it? >> Something like that. >> done a good job. Um, you know, I'm not sure we'll see him this week, but I would see him helping us down the road. So yeah, he's done a really good job. He's got to You know, you forget he's played. He's He's a smart player. He's very mature. Um, and he's constantly trying to learn, picking our brains, talking, and he has stayed really locked in. I really love the way he's approached it. Um, and I will be excited for when he does get his opportunity. >> What What is the update on Trey Moore? Um, we've seen him rehabbing. Obviously, we thought it was an ankle injury. I think it was an ankle injury. Is Is it Was it one of the ankle injuries that's a little bit more serious than than others? >> I mean, serious enough where he's been out. You know, some ankle injuries you're back in a few weeks, um a month. I mean, obviously it was more serious because of the time that has passed, that he's not back. Um I'm hopeful that we'll have him back at some point this year playing. And I am still hopeful on that. That's the best update I can give you cuz I'm really not sure of a timeline there. >> What's the uh what's the Chris Bell thing I just did practice on Wednesday >> Yeah, just in practice. Um he got hit in his leg. Um so nothing again, I reiterate that nothing major. It does not have to do with his prior injury. Um we'll see if he can go on Sunday and I do not um expect this to be a long-term thing cuz I know that question will come up. All right guys, have a great Friday. >> Thank you.

title: Jerry Jones says 18-game NFL season is 'inevitable' | Pro Football Talk
text: Speaking of Jerry, topic two. It's always worth listening to the full 20 to 25 minutes that Jerry Jones spends twice per week on 1053 The Fan in Dallas on Friday. And I've noticed a rhythm, and I think it's smart. The hosts tend to get Jerry with the potentially juicy stuff later in the session. You don't want to throw the thing off the rails early. You don't want to ask him a question that's maybe going to get him upset. You wait till the very end. And he was asked near the end of Friday's visit about 18 games. And I think it was kind of a followup how it came up. I don't think they were planning to ask him that one, but they asked him about 18 games and what he thought about when the NFL would move to 18 games. And he said, "It's not very far away. Next month, no. Next year, maybe. The next year, maybe." And I think it's worth reminding everyone how the NFL can get to 18 games. And Jerry mentioned this, there has to be an agreement with the NFL Players Association. He also said it's in everyone's best interest. Well, the players may say it's not in our best interest to play 18 games. It's in our collective best interest to realize greater revenue that would get shared via the salary cap to all of the players. But per player, the difference from having an 18th game, not nearly as significant as it will be for the 32 owners. So, it's much more in their interest. I just look at it this way. It's very simple. One side is clamoring for 18 games. The other side isn't saying anything about 18 games. If anything, they're saying, "Hey, hey, hey, easy, buddy." Now, that's under the current management. Remember a couple of years ago before everything went sideways for Lloyd Howell. He made that ridiculous comment. I think it was a Mike Jones interview with The Athletic where he said, "Who doesn't want more football?" Me included. That's not how you maximize your leverage. But the bottom line is there needs to be an agreement. We're not going to get to 18 until there's an agreement. And now that JC Treader's in charge, he's made it clear he's in no hurry. And the NFL is frustrated by this. As I've said earlier this year, the league's position is that their business has been constipated. That was the sourc's quote, not mine, by the turmoil at the NFL Players Association. The whole Lloyd Howell resignation, David White serving as the interim executive director, the election of JC Treader, now he's got to get up to speed. It keeps progress from happening for the collective business of the NFL that is essentially driven by the league and the union. So when Jerry says next month, no, well, of course not. They're not going to add an 18th game for 2026, that that that's some things don't need to be said, and that's one of them. Can they add one by 2027? In theory, yes. But they've already picked the date for the Super Bowl and they're moving forward with it. That was why they waited as long as they did to pick the day in February, I believe it's the 13th in 2028 when the Super Bowl will be played in Atlanta. If they were to add another game now, they'd have to either start the season a week early or they'd have to eliminate the week off between the conference championship games and the Super Bowl. And they've done that before. They did that for 911. If you add a by-week, which more than a few players have said, "Hey, if we go to 18 games, we need a second by week." If you do that, you have to do both. You got to start Labor Day weekend, and you got to get rid of the dead week between the conference championships and the Super Bowl. So, it's possible by 2027, but I don't think it's ideal. I don't think the NFL is that hellbent on getting to 18 games that they would take away the two week lag time between the conference championships and the Super Bowl and start the season on Labor Day weekend. They don't want to start the season on Labor Day weekend. Now, I think they should explore it because nowadays you're still going to get your ratings points. You're still going to get your viewership because people are going to be watching the games on their phones wherever they are. That was the whole idea. It's the last unofficial weekend of summer. People are at home. They're at barbecues. They're at family reunions. They're traveling. Well, if you play on Liberty now, somebody's going to have the TV set up with the Wi-Fi pulled off of the satellite dish. Boom. You got all the games. or you're going to have a bunch of people's phones set up and each one's going to be on a different game on Sunday ticket. So, they could do it if they had to, but that's the only way it happens by 2027. I guess it could happen by 2028. I don't believe they've got a firm date for the Super Bowl that caps the 2028 season. It's going to happen at some point, I think, between 2028 and 2031. 2031 is the first year after the current CBA. The current labor deal expires in March of 2031 after the completion of the 2030 season. And you know, there's two ways to do this. They can do this the easy way or the hard way. They did it the hard way in 2011. Now, it wasn't about the length of the season then. It was about how they carve up the pie. It was about the owners clawing back some of the gains that the players made in the 2006 CBA. 2020 they did it the easy way in theory they worked out a deal in advance but it was hard for former executive director Demores Smith to get the deal through because a lot of the players didn't want to agree to 17 games and a lot of players voted against the CBA that was agreed to in 2020 because of 17 games because I think the average player doesn't understand how this plays out if at the end of the Hey, the league is determined to have 18 games and they are. CBA expires. What happens? Players get locked out like they did in 2011. Players get locked out until they cry uncle. And they'll cry uncle as to 18 regular season games and as to 16 annual international games. The league is going to get what they want. So, they either get what they want a few years early or they're forced to go through the motions of the lockout and get the players to eventually say, "Okay." And an offseason lockout isn't good for anyone, even if games aren't missed. And the only game that was missed in 2011 was the Hall of Fame game, which I would regard as a positive. But even then, it creates all sorts of uncertainty and turmoil. And there were stories of guys going out and taking out loans at ridiculously high rates and it created financial issues and it slowed down free agency. They want free agency to begin. The players do as they should as early as possible because you get you get your signing bonuses. You start making your money. You get some certainty about where you're going to be. So if the union pushes this all the way to March of 2031, they're asking for a lockout. My guess is once JC Treader has gotten himself sufficiently comfortable in the position of executive director, then they'll embark on trying to work out a deal. But he's got to be sure that enough players will understand why you do a deal early. And he needs to explain it the way I'm talking about it right now. Hey guys, I know you don't want to play 18 games, but here's what you got to ask yourself. Come 2031, the issue isn't 18 games or 17 games. The issue is 18 games or zero games. Are you willing? Are you content? Are you prepared to not make any money in 2031? And I think the more the players understand that ahead of time, they'll recognize, okay, this is which way the wind is blowing. Even then, they may decide to be a little stubborn and they may decide to play this thing out. And who knows, maybe the players by the time 2030 run rolls around with guys who have made good money in college and maybe if the union starts getting the message to the college players about saving their money in advance of a potential lockout in 2031, maybe they'll be ready to fight. That's the fundamental problem. There's an imbalance between the owner's willingness to use the nuclear option of shutting down a season and the players unwillingness to miss a game check. And that's one of the arguments I make from time to time to the fans out there who are so quick to line up behind the billionaires. One side is willing to take football away from you for an entire season. The other side isn't. So why do you rally around the ones who would take football away from you for a full year? Why why do you do that? The players now the players aren't acting out of altruism. The players are acting out of self-interest, but their interest is to play. Your interest is to watch them play. The owner's interest is to squeeze them until they cry uncle. And if that means giving up a full season, oh well, that's life. It'll be back the year after that and it'll continue. See, that's I think the biggest difference. When you own the business, you own it 10 years, 20 years, 30 years until you sell or die. Players have a finite window. And if you would have a year without football, you've got all these veterans that haven't played. You got a bunch of rookies coming in who played the prior year in college. Hell, they may start grabbing up the roster spots. And if there's acrimony and hard feelings, you can have teams more inclined to move on from some of these veterans, some of the veterans who maybe were too vocal in the effort to stand firm and fight. These are all realistic considerations. But back to the point that is the most pressing the NFL talks about, not collectively, but individuals, Robert Craft has done this, now Jerry Jones has done it. They talk about 18 games as as if it's a given. It's not. It'll probably happen, but it's not nearly as easy as they seem to make it. They just gloss over the fact that there will be some degree of a fight. And it may be a fight that the players are willing to take all the way through to regular season games being missed. I doubt it, but it could still
